---
title: "Quiz: curves as level sets"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Convention: the curve is where $\phi = 0$, with $\phi < 0$ inside.

---

**Q1.** $\phi(x, y) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} - 2$. Is the point $(1, 1)$ inside or outside the curve? How far is it from the curve?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Evaluate $\phi$ and look at the sign. This $\phi$ is a signed distance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\phi(1, 1) = \sqrt 2 - 2 = -0.59$: inside, 0.59 from the circle (because this $\phi$ is the signed distance, $|\phi|$ is the distance).
:::

---

**Q2.** You have $\phi_A$ for a disk and $\phi_B$ for a square. Which function describes "the disk with the square cut out of it"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Cutting out = inside $A$ and inside the complement of $B$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\max(\phi_A, -\phi_B)$: $-\phi_B$ is negative outside the square (the complement), and $\max$ is the intersection.
:::

---

**Q3.** Two disks of radius 1 at $(\pm 1.2, 0)$ are combined with $\min$. For which levels $c$ is the contour $\phi = c$ one curve, and for which two?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Find $\phi$ at the point between the disks.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At the origin $\phi = 1.2 - 1 = 0.2$, the lowest point of the gap between the two "valleys". For $-1 < c < 0.2$ the contour is two circles of radius $1 + c$; for $c > 0.2$ the circles overlap and the contour is one curve. The function is the same; only the cut changes.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why is $\nabla\phi$ perpendicular to the curve $\phi = 0$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How does $\phi$ change when you walk along the curve?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Along the curve $\phi$ stays 0, so its rate of change in the tangent direction is zero: $\nabla\phi \cdot \mathbf t = 0$. The gradient therefore has no tangential component; it points across the curve, towards larger $\phi$ (outward).
:::

---

**Q5.** What is the curvature of a circle of radius 4? Of a straight line? Which sign does a dent (a concave part of the inside) have?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\kappa = 1/r$ for a circle with the inside convex.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1/4 = 0.25$; a line has $\kappa = 0$. In a dent the normals converge instead of spreading out: $\kappa < 0$.
:::

---

**Q6.** $\phi_1 = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} - 1$ and $\phi_2 = 5\phi_1$. Do they describe the same curve? Which one is a signed distance function, and what is $|\nabla\phi_2|$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Scaling does not move the zero set.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Same curve (the unit circle), same normals, same curvature. Only $\phi_1$ is a signed distance ($|\nabla\phi_1| = 1$); $|\nabla\phi_2| = 5$, so $|\phi_2|$ overstates the distance five times.
:::

---

**Q7.** A signed distance function is the distance transform with a sign. Where on the grid can $|\nabla\phi| = 1$ fail?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of the middle of a rectangle: which boundary point is nearest?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Where two (or more) boundary points are equally near: the "ridge" or medial axis inside a shape (the diagonals of a square, the centre of a disk). There the distance has a kink, the gradient jumps and finite differences give a smaller $|\nabla\phi|$ and a very large curvature.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* For a signed distance function, show that $\kappa = \nabla^2\phi$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Start from $\kappa = \nabla\cdot(\nabla\phi/|\nabla\phi|)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With $|\nabla\phi| = 1$ the normal is $\nabla\phi$ itself, so $\kappa = \nabla\cdot\nabla\phi = \phi_{xx} + \phi_{yy} = \nabla^2\phi$. (Check on the circle: $\phi = \rho - r$ has $\nabla^2\phi = 1/\rho$.)
:::
